title: Parking
summary: How to park on level streets and hills, parallel and angle park, leave a space safely, and know where parking is never allowed.

items: Automatic transmission: shift into Park and set the parking brake.
Manual (stick-shift) transmission: leave it in gear, first or reverse, and set the parking brake.
Before you walk away: turn off the engine, take the key with you and lock the doors.

blocks.text: Set the parking brake every time you park, even on flat ground. It is your backup if the transmission slips.
Turn your front wheels so that if the car starts to roll, it rolls into the curb or off the road instead of into traffic. Then set the parking brake.

rows: Turn the wheels toward the curb.
Turn the wheels away from the curb, then let the car roll back slowly until the front tire rests against the curb.
Turn the wheels toward the shoulder (to the right), so the car would roll away from traffic.
Turn the wheels so the car would not roll into the street.

blocks.caption: Uphill with a curb: front wheels turned away from the curb.
Downhill with a curb: front wheels turned toward the curb.
Uphill with no curb: front wheels turned toward the edge of the road.

blocks.text: The same logic works on either side of the street. On a one-way street, if you park along the left curb facing downhill, turn your wheels to the left, toward that curb.
In a manual car on a hill, handbooks recommend first (low) gear when facing uphill and reverse when facing downhill, plus the parking brake.

items: Check traffic behind you and turn on your signal (right signal for a space on the right).
Pull up beside the car parked ahead of the space, about two feet away from it, with your rear bumpers about even.
Look back over your shoulder and back up slowly, turning the steering wheel sharply to the right, toward the curb.
When your front end clears the car ahead, turn the wheel to the left as you keep backing.
Straighten the wheels and pull forward or back to center your car in the space, close to the curb.

blocks.text: If your right rear tire bumps the curb before the car is in, you probably held the wheel to the right too long. Pull out and try again.
A backup camera helps, but it is not enough. Turn and look behind you, and use the camera and mirrors only as aids.
How close to the curb you must park varies by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Watch for traffic ahead and behind, and for pedestrians, then signal.
Slow down and make sure the rear of your car will clear the parked vehicles as you swing in.
Steer into the center of the space and stop before your front tires reach the curb or parking block.
Straighten your wheels so the car is centered.

blocks.text: When backing out of a straight-in (perpendicular) space, back slowly and keep looking behind you. Start turning the steering wheel once your front bumper clears the car beside you.
Remember how a car moves in reverse: if you turn so the rear swings to the right, the front swings the opposite way, to the left. Watch your front end so it does not hit the car next to you.

sections.heading: Pulling out of a parking space

items: Signal to show you are pulling out.
Check your mirrors and look over your shoulder for cars, bicycles and motorcycles.
Go only when there is a safe gap.

blocks.text: The driver leaving a parking space must yield to traffic already in the lane. Most crashes between parked cars and moving traffic are caused by a driver pulling away from the curb carelessly.
If you are parked tightly, back up close to the car behind you first. That gives you room to signal and steer out in one smooth move.

Never open a door on the traffic side until it is safe. Check your mirrors and look back for bicycles, motorcycles and cars first. A person who opens a door into traffic can be held liable for the crash it causes.

blocks.caption: Look back before opening a door on the traffic side: a bicyclist may be coming.

items: When you can, get out on the curb side, especially passengers.
If you must get out on the street side, wait for a clear gap and close the door as soon as you are out.

blocks.text: Use the Dutch Reach: open the door with your far hand (your right hand from the driver's seat). This turns your body so you naturally look back for anyone coming.

items: On a sidewalk.
On a crosswalk, marked or unmarked. A corner where the sidewalk meets the street is an unmarked crosswalk even without painted lines.
Inside an intersection.
On railroad tracks.
On a bridge or overpass, or in a tunnel, unless signs allow it.
In a bike lane.
In front of a driveway, even for a few minutes.
Double parked: on the street side of a vehicle already parked at the curb.
In a disabled parking space without a valid placard or plate, even if you stay in the car with the engine running.
In the striped (crosshatched) area beside a disabled space. That space is for wheelchairs and lifts.
Wherever signs or curb markings prohibit it.

blocks.text: A disability placard belongs to the person, not the car. You may use it only when that person is with you. Borrowing a relative's car does not let you use their placard.
You may stop inside an intersection or on a crosswalk only to avoid a crash or when a police officer tells you to.
Minimum distances from fire hydrants, crosswalks, stop signs, railroad crossings and fire station driveways, and the meaning of curb colors, vary by state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.

sections.heading: Parking on the street and at night

items: On a two-way street, park facing the same direction as the traffic in the lane next to you.
Parking lights show other drivers where a stopped or parked vehicle is. They are not for driving.
If you must leave your car along an unlit road at night, leave your parking lights or hazard flashers on so others can see it.

keyPoints: Automatic: Park plus parking brake. Manual: in gear plus parking brake. Take your key and lock up.
On hills: downhill toward the curb, uphill away from the curb, no curb toward the shoulder.
Parallel park by lining up rear bumpers, backing sharply toward the curb, then turning the other way once your front clears.
When leaving a space, signal, check mirrors and over your shoulder, and yield to traffic.
Check behind before opening a door; the Dutch Reach makes you look.
Never park on sidewalks, crosswalks, railroad tracks, bridges or in bike lanes, in intersections, in front of driveways or double parked.
Disabled spaces and their striped aisles are only for vehicles with a valid placard or plate, and the placard holder must be present.
Parking distances and curb colors vary by state; check your State Cheat Sheet.
